title: Adaptive handoff rate controller for attention kernel selection (v2/v3)
creator: Amina Rao
description:
Summary: We see oscillatory kernel switching between FlashAttn v2 and v3 during bursts and long-context workloads. Symptoms include transient p95 token latency spikes, increased workspace allocation churn, and occasional OOM-avoidant evictions that increase end-to-end decode time. Root cause hypothesis: the current binary/threshold based handoff triggers on instantaneous signals (matrix shape + occupancy) without smoothing for workload variance and memory pressure. This causes the runtime to flip kernels when batch composition changes, especially during mixed short/long requests and prefill-heavy bursts.

Proposal: Implement an Adaptive Handoff Rate Controller (AHRC) that smooths kernel selection transitions and enforces a controlled slew-rate for moving traffic weight between v2 and v3. Key signals: per-model stability score (recent latency variance), short-term burstiness (requests/s), GPU memory pressure, and per-layer compatibility heuristics. The controller will expose tunables: max_weight_delta_per_second, hysteresis_window_ms, stability_threshold, and emergency_fallback_threshold. The default algorithm is a proportional-slew filter with an optional derivative term to damp oscillation. The AHRC will operate at the model-instance level and maintain lightweight state that survives hot restarts.

Goals and success metrics: reduce kernel-switch rate by >=75% under mixed workloads; eliminate transient p95 token latency spikes >20% over baseline; keep average end-to-end decode latency within 5% of current baseline for steady-state traffic. Safety targets: auto-rollback on sustained p95 regressions >20% for 5 minutes or error rate increases >1% absolute.

Implementation phases: 1) Telemetry-only probe (2 weeks) — compute per-model stability score and emit a new metric series (kernel_switch_rate, per-model_latency_variance, handoff_weight_ts). 2) Simulated offline evaluator (1 week) — run AHRC logic against historical traces in the prober harness to validate parameters. 3) Canary runtime rollout (3 weeks) — feature flagged on 10% of traffic, observe SLOs and evictions, iterate. 4) Gradual rollout with staged gating to 100% with automated rollback.

Technical notes: AHRC will be implemented as a runtime scheduling module with C++ hotpath code for weight updates, and a thin Python control plane to expose UI flags and telemetry aggregation. For low-latency we will avoid per-request RPCs and instead compute weight adjustments on a short timer (e.g., 200ms). The module must integrate with the kernel-prober and allocator to avoid increasing memory fragmentation.

Risks and mitigations: 1) Mis-tuned slew leads to slow adaptation — mitigate via canary with synthetic bursts and backoff. 2) Hidden per-layer incompatibilities — add per-layer conservative masks and test harness with replayed long-context samples. 3) Monitoring blindspots — add derived metrics (kernel_switch_rate_by_layer, p95_delta_post_switch) and alert on regressions.

Deliverables: design doc link, prober harness changes, runtime module PR, telemetry dashboards, rollout runbook, and post-rollout regression report.
